A beautiful mind comes to mind. Wait, does that relate? No, this is text. Not crazy yet.

This explains a lot of "spooky" coincidences. Our brains are wired to find meaningful patterns and there's no evolutionary reason to eliminate false positives. If you see a face in the bushes and you run away, nine times out of ten it's nothing, but it doesn't cost you anything except some calories from the running. But if you don't run the one time it is a predator, you're dead, game over, so we are biased toward seeing things that aren't actually there.

Edit: spelling
I personally like the hidden faces brand of pareidolia. Faces are so important to us that our brain can't help but see them places.

According to the Wikipedia entry, what you've described is actually called Pareidolia, which is a specific type of apophany. Apophany is generally just perceiving patterns or connections in random or meaningless information.

Sometimes I've noticed my mind listening along to far off music. Then after several minutes realize that there is no music, it was just my mind thinking it was 'hearing' patterns and assuming it was music, but it was just random repeating patterns white noise.

Degree MotionSENSE Motion Activated Anti-Perspirant & Deodorant? Can a sprayed on piece of scented chalky mush really tell when you're moving more and act accordingly?

Antiperspirants work by clogging your sweat glands with small bits of aluminum. Assuming you put more than one swipe on, there will be a layer that sits on your skin. As you move around, your skin will stretch and compress, which will allow more of the aluminum bits to fill your pores. So technically it's not bullshit, but this is something all antiperspirants do, it's very misleading of them to advertise it as some exclusive formula or whatever.

I'm looking to move in about a year and wanted to move to a bicycle city. These are my main priorities:

Paved path bicycling (my fav route is Chicago/urban cycling for commuting and such)

Public Trans OR minimal car traffic

Mild Winters (not a fan of snow, but maybe willing to deal with it if it was worth it. Scrapping a windshield daily is different then shoveling the driveway daily)

Low taxes (either low sales and okay income or no income and higher sales tax)

I live in Florida right now. And the heckling drivers make it not enjoyable to ride. In Chicago, I loved the freedom it gave me. But talk about a city that just wants your money.
Best place in America to move for cycling?
Portland checks most of those boxes except winter weather is pretty crappy, although no snow.
That's what I was thinking. It's actually my first choice, but I wanted I see what others thought.

Just a heads-up about portland. There's actually an Oregon state law which specifically deals with banning cyclists from 4 specific sections of highway in Portland and 1 section of interstate 5 in Medford. So you're gonna want to check into that if you do move to Portland.
There is also Colorado. Boulder, Longmont and Denver are all great cycling areas.
Do they have good public trans or good traffic?

I would second Northern Colorado, and also add Tucson, Arizona to the list. It's a huge cycling hub, check it out if you get a chance.
I was wondering about the southwest. I haven't heard a ton, but I am guessing that's due to the population?

Tucson is a relatively small city, so you probably won't hear too much about it, but just an hour and a half or so North you run into the Phoenix area, which is massive and still growing fast. Further North you have some great little towns like Prescott, Payson, Sedona, and Flagstaff (not so little), all of which are great for taking a weekend off up in the mountains.

Tucson also has good public transportation (U of A is there, lots of college students), and obviously mild winters, though the summers are very hot.
